case_study_insert.main_stem: Havenwell Physio Group (HPG) is a private limited company in the healthcare equipment sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2013 by Priya Raval, the business supplies adjustable treatment tables to private clinics and operates with democratic leadership in a hierarchical structure. HPG plans to invest $640,000 in a new automated treatment-table assembly line with recycled aluminium frames, financed by a $400,000 seven-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $85 a unit and a selling price of $145, and currently produces 10,000 units a year. HPG faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8% and the assembly line has reported a rising defect rate in welded frames.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: HPG assembled 2,400 treatment tables last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints about uneven welds fell from 17 to 6 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 4.1 days. Market research of 300 clinic buyers found that 68% would pay up to $6 more for tables with recycled aluminium frames, and 55% check environmental credentials before ordering.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Havenwell Physio Group for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.2% to 5.1%. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.50 to $14.28 per hour from April 2027. (3) Aluminium and steel input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, healthcare equipment inflation is 6.3%, and consumer spending on medical equipment grew 2.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: HPG is funding part of its $640,000 assembly line with a $400,000 seven-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HPG of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or capital repayments, so the $240,000 contributed from internal funds costs HPG nothing to service. Every dollar not paid as interest on the $400,000 seven-year loan remains inside the business to absorb the $240,000 a year fixed costs, which is valuable while 8% absenteeism and a rising defect rate in welded frames are already disrupting output of 10,000 units. This protects cash flow and the $145 selling price from short-term pressure.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps control with Priya Raval and the existing shareholders because no outside lender can attach conditions to how the new recycled-aluminium line is run. There is no collateral at risk of repossession if clinic demand for treatment tables disappoints, and no new lender to satisfy, so HPG can rebuild the 1,050 revenue line and tackle the weld complaints on its own timetable while preserving the full benefit of the expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to HPG, its costs and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: HPG is launching its new recycled-aluminium treatment tables. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HPG choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV advert would build awareness of the recycled-aluminium tables among private clinics nationwide very quickly, giving the $640,000 assembly line a strong launch. However, airtime and production are extremely costly for a 40-employee firm already servicing a $400,000 loan, and most viewers are not clinical buyers, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is much cheaper and suits a time-limited launch message, and it can reach clinics in HPG's home region where deliveries already average 4.1 days. Its weakness is narrow geographic reach: the business supplies private clinics more widely, so radio alone cannot generate the 10,000-unit volume needed to cover $240,000 fixed costs.

Social media influencer marketing: Physiotherapy and clinic-management influencers can demonstrate the adjustable frames directly to the buying audience. This is measurable and low cost per contact, and it lets HPG tell the story that 68% of 300 surveyed clinic buyers would pay $6 more for recycled frames and 55% check environmental credentials — turning the research in Appendix 1 into a precise message.

Recommendation: HPG should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the exact clinic buyers identified in the survey, is far cheaper than television and reaches further than local radio, while reinforcing the recycled-aluminium premium. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a $400,000-loan-funded launch, and radio is rejected as too geographically narrow for a supplier aiming at 10,000 units a year.

It also avoids the heavy wastage of spend that a broad television campaign would create for a specialist clinical product bought by a relatively small group of clinic managers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to HPG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HPG with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed analysis of all three options in the context of HPG with a justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: HPG's absenteeism has reached 8% and welded-frame defects are rising. Explain two benefits for HPG of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its assembly team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 40 employees a real voice in how the new assembly line is organised, so they feel valued and are more willing to attend regularly. Since absenteeism has reached 8%, involving welders in setting shift patterns and frame-handling routines addresses the cause of lost time directly, protecting the 10,000-unit output target and the 2,400 tables assembled last quarter.

Point 2: Consulting the people who actually weld the frames generates practical ideas for reducing the 2.2% defect rate, for example better jigs or ordering of recycled aluminium stock. Higher involvement raises commitment and reduces the complaints that fell from 17 to 6 per month, so quality improves at source instead of relying on inspection, and the hierarchical structure benefits from front-line knowledge that senior managers do not have.

The resulting fall in rework also frees capacity to meet the 4.1-day order fulfilment promise to private clinics.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to HPG's absenteeism, defect rate and output.

questions.question_text: HPG wants to cut its 2.2% defect rate on welded frames and reduce 8% absenteeism. Consider introducing quality circles or paying a performance-related bonus for weld quality. Which should HPG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality circles: Small groups of welders meeting regularly to identify and solve frame-weld problems fit HPG's democratic style and the 2.2% defect rate. They use the workers' own knowledge, are inexpensive, and can also improve attendance because staff feel heard. They take time to produce results and need trained facilitators, and they do not by themselves reward the individual effort needed on the new line.

Performance-related bonus: Paying extra for defect-free welds gives a direct financial incentive and could quickly lower the 17-to-6 monthly complaint count and the 3.6% defect rate of a year ago. The weakness is cost and measurement: HPG would have to judge each welder's output fairly, and a bonus focused only on welds may ignore the 8% absenteeism problem or encourage rushing elsewhere.

Decision: HPG should introduce quality circles first. They attack the weld problem at source, are affordable for a 40-employee firm funding a $640,000 expansion, and support the democratic leadership already in the stem; the bonus can be added later once reliable quality data exist. The bonus is rejected as costly to administer and narrow, because it rewards weld quality without tackling the absenteeism that disrupts the 2,400 tables assembled each quarter.

A further consideration is cost control: HPG is already committing $240,000 of retained profit and servicing a $400,000 loan, so a bonus paid every quarter would be harder to sustain than time spent in short team meetings. Quality circles also build problem-solving habits that remain useful after the new assembly line is installed, whereas a bonus stops influencing behaviour as soon as payment stops. For these reasons the circles are the more durable answer to the welded-frame complaints, provided managers act on the suggestions made.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two approaches with limited application to HPG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of HPG.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluation of both approaches with a justified decision covering cost, quality data and motivation, explaining why the alternative is rejected.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HPG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($145 − $85) = $240,000 ÷ $60 = 4,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 4,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $145 − $85 = $60. Answer: contribution per unit is $60.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HPG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 4,000-unit break-even output with 10,000 units produced: the margin of safety is 6,000 units, showing the clamp table line is profitable and how far clinic demand could fall before a loss.
2. Use the $60 contribution per unit to model pricing: a discount to $139 would cut contribution to $54, so about 4,445 units would be needed to cover $240,000 fixed costs, helping judge whether a bulk hospital order is worthwhile.
3. Average total cost is $109 a unit ($240,000 ÷ 10,000 = $24 plus $85), below the $145 price, which sets a floor for negotiations with private clinics and shows the cushion against the 9.6% input-cost rise.
4. Labour productivity is 250 units per worker (10,000 ÷ 40), a benchmark for the new automated line; if welding defects and 8% absenteeism are cut, output per worker should rise, and managers can track this each quarter.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 4,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $60 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 6,000 units against 10,000 units output; discount modelling to $139 cutting contribution to $54; average total cost of $109 against the $145 price; and labour productivity of 250 units per worker to track absenteeism and defects.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HPG's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has HPG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.0%

Detailed workings:
2024: revenue 900, cost of sales 540, gross profit 360; 2025: revenue 1,050, cost of sales 588, gross profit 462. Operating profit rose from 135 to 189 and capital employed from 750 to 900. Interest payable moved from 20 to 24.

Evaluation: The margins show a clear improvement. The trading margin rose from 40.0% to 44.0% because cost of sales grew more slowly than revenue, so each dollar of clinic sales leaves more gross profit. The operating margin improved from 15.0% to 18.0%, meaning the $240,000 fixed costs and the weld problems were absorbed more efficiently as revenue reached 1,050. Return on the larger capital base rose from 18.0% to 21.0%, so the money already tied up in the business, including the new assembly line, is earning more, which is a healthy sign before the $640,000 expansion.

Conclusion: HPG's financial position has improved. All three measures are higher in 2025, so both trading profitability and the efficiency of capital use have strengthened. The business is therefore better placed to service the $400,000 bank loan, although the rising interest payable and the 9.6% rise in aluminium and steel costs mean the margin gains must be protected.

The movement in gross profit from 360 to 462 also shows the benefit of tighter control over production costs while treatment-table output remained strong.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of margin and capital trends and a justified conclusion on whether HPG's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HPG of introducing recycled aluminium frames for its treatment tables.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The Appendix 1 research shows 68% of 300 clinic buyers would pay up to $6 more for tables with recycled aluminium frames and 55% check environmental credentials. That premium would lift the $60 contribution per unit toward $66 and help protect the improved trading margin shown in Appendix 2 against the 9.6% rise in aluminium and steel costs, while differentiating HPG from suppliers of standard tables and supporting the launch of the $640,000 line.

Disadvantage: Recycled aluminium may cost more or be less consistent than virgin metal, pushing the $85 variable cost per unit up and squeezing contribution if the full $6 premium is not accepted by clinics. Any weakness in the recycled frames could also worsen the 2.2% defect rate in welded frames, adding rework when absenteeism is already 8% and delaying the 4.1-day order fulfilment time.

HPG should also verify the supply and consistency of recycled aluminium before promising delivery dates to clinics.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to HPG's research, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.1%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase to $14.28 and the 9.6% rise in aluminium and steel input costs will affect HPG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.2% to 5.1%): If the $400,000 seven-year bank loan is variable-rate, the increase is 0.9 percentage points, so 0.009 × $400,000 = $3,600 a year. That is modest beside $240,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. HPG can reduce this risk by agreeing a fixed rate, so this is a manageable rather than decisive change.

Minimum wage rise (5.8% to $14.28): The insert gives no hours worked or base pay for the 40 staff, so no honest annual wage total can be invented. The defensible judgement is qualitative: the whole payroll becomes more expensive while output must stay near 10,000 units to cover $240,000 fixed costs, so unit labour cost will rise unless the new automated line lifts the 250 units-per-worker productivity figure. HPG may need modest price increases, restrained by the $145 selling price and clinic competition.

Input cost rise (9.6% aluminium and steel): As an explicitly labelled upper bound, if the entire $85 variable cost were exposed, 0.096 × $85 = $8.16 per unit; at 10,000 units that is $81,600 a year, cutting contribution from $60 to about $51.84. Even a smaller pass-through would erode the $6 premium that 68% of surveyed buyers accept, so HPG must renegotiate with clinics or absorb part of the rise.

Conclusion: The 9.6% input-cost rise has the greatest impact because it applies to every one of the 10,000 units and directly attacks the $60 contribution that funds the $640,000 expansion. The interest rise is only $3,600 a year and the wage effect is spread and uncertain, so neither threatens margins as immediately as material costs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to HPG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on HPG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a justified greatest-impact judgment with reasons for rejecting the other two.
